Liberty CTI Open Source Analysis — For Texas Industry Situational Awareness UNCLASSIFIED // OPEN SOURCE // PROPRIETARY
CISA/NSA/FBI/DC3 and 19 partner agencies attribute decade-plus router-exploitation campaign to Russia’s FSB Center 16 — energy, finance, and DIB named directly DOJ unseals indictment against Medialand/ML.Cloud bulletproof hosting operators — infrastructure tied to LockBit, Cl0p, BlackSuit, and Play ransomware, $62M+ in victim losses CISA adds actively-exploited SonicWall SMA1000 flaws (CVSS 10.0) to KEV catalog — second confirmed edge-device vector this week, unrelated actor CISA/NSA/FBI/DC3 and 19 partner agencies attribute decade-plus router-exploitation campaign to Russia’s FSB Center 16 — energy, finance, and DIB named directly DOJ unseals indictment against Medialand/ML.Cloud bulletproof hosting operators — infrastructure tied to LockBit, Cl0p, BlackSuit, and Play ransomware, $62M+ in victim losses CISA adds actively-exploited SonicWall SMA1000 flaws (CVSS 10.0) to KEV catalog — second confirmed edge-device vector this week, unrelated actor

Executive Warning: This week’s evidence points to one problem, showing up three separate times: basic front-door security — on network equipment, on remote-access systems, and inside the federal government’s own reporting process — isn’t being managed, and attackers are walking through the gaps. A 19-agency, 13-country warning tied a years-long Russian intelligence campaign to a simple failure: routers left with factory-default passwords, the network equivalent of never changing the lock code the vendor ships with. Days later, a second, unrelated attacker was caught actively breaking into a different piece of common business equipment — the kind employees use to connect to the office network from home. And the same week federal officials told everyone to set up a proper process for outside researchers to report security problems, we learned that when someone tried to report a problem to the government itself, it took nine emails before anyone answered. Separately, as background and not as new evidence, the U.S. and Iran exchanged deadly fire this week, with American service members killed. That raises the stakes on a threat we’ve been watching, but it hasn’t yet produced any actual evidence of a cyberattack. This week’s real, provable warning is about doors left unlocked, not doors that might get kicked in.

Board Implications This Week — Ask

Can we name, right now, the one person who owns our list of internet-connected network equipment, and the one person who owns handling an outside security report? “IT handles it” is not a real answer.

Board Implications This Week — Direct

Order a count of every router, firewall, and remote-access device connected to the internet this week, and confirm who has the authority to unplug one if it’s found compromised.

Board Implications This Week — Document

Keep a written, dated record of who checked what and decided what — a paper trail showing leadership actually looked at this problem, with names attached.

Board Implications This Week — Rehearse

Actually test your process for an outside person to report a security problem — don’t just publish an email address and assume it works. The federal government’s own version of that address didn’t work.

Dominant Geo-Cyber Judgment

Liberty CTI’s call this week: the threat isn’t sophistication, it’s neglect. HIGH CONFIDENCE Three separate, confirmed cases this week show attackers getting in through basic, fixable oversights rather than clever hacking. Russian intelligence used factory-default passwords on network routers — nothing more advanced than that. A second, unrelated attacker broke into remote-access equipment through a known flaw the vendor had already warned about. And the federal government’s own security team missed a researcher’s warning about exposed cloud credentials for over a week, days before publishing guidance telling everyone else how to handle exactly that situation.

The takeaway for Texas organizations: if your network equipment still has factory settings, if remote-access systems aren’t kept current, or if there’s no clear person responsible for handling an outside security report, you carry the same exposure these three cases just demonstrated. That is our judgment about the pattern, not a confirmed fact about any specific Texas organization — we have not identified a named Texas victim in any of these three cases.

Bottom line: On Iran, we’re holding our position from last month. MODERATE CONFIDENCE Iran has reason to want to strike back at U.S. infrastructure, and this week’s combat losses make that motive stronger — but wanting to and doing it are different things, and we don’t yet have evidence of the second. We will change our assessment the moment that evidence shows up, not before. Act on what’s proven this week: the unlocked doors.

Section I

What Changed This Week

Russian Intelligence Exploited Routers Left With Factory Passwords

On 13 July 2026, the NSA, CISA, the FBI, and 19 partner agencies across 13 countries published a joint warning: Russian government hackers — the FSB, Russia’s intelligence service — have spent years breaking into routers and network equipment simply by trying the default password the device shipped with, then quietly copying the device’s settings to a remote server. No hacking tool, no malware, no sophistication required — just an unlocked door. The industries named directly include phone and internet providers, defense contractors, power companies, banks, government offices, and hospitals.

A Second, Separate Attack Hit Remote-Access Equipment

On 14 July 2026, SonicWall — a maker of equipment many businesses use to let employees connect securely from home — confirmed that attackers were actively exploiting a serious flaw in that equipment, letting them take full control of the device. This is a different, unrelated attacker from the Russian router campaign above. The significance: two separate attackers, in the same week, both got in through the same kind of weak spot — equipment sitting on the edge of the network that wasn’t locked down.

Feds Charged the Landlords Behind Major Ransomware Gangs

On 14 July 2026, the Department of Justice charged three Russian nationals and two Russia-based companies with running what security professionals call “bulletproof hosting” — essentially, renting out server space to criminals and refusing to shut it down no matter who complains, the internet equivalent of a landlord who rents rooms to a crime ring and looks the other way. This hosting operation is tied to more than $62 million in losses and supported several of the ransomware gangs behind major hospital, school, and bank attacks over the past few years.

The Government Told Everyone to Fix a Problem It Had Just Failed at Itself

On 15 July 2026, CISA and several international partners published guidance telling organizations to set up a real, working process for outside security researchers to report problems. Six days earlier, CISA admitted that a researcher who found the agency’s own cloud passwords sitting exposed online had to send nine emails, with no response, before anyone at CISA acted. In its own words, the agency’s reporting channels “were not well defined.” It is a real-world example, at the highest level, of exactly the mistake the new guidance is meant to prevent.

Iran-U.S. Conflict Escalation — Background, Not a New Cyber Finding

U.S. military officials confirmed two American service members killed in Jordan on 17 July and a third killed in Iraq on 18–19 July, with a fourth death still being confirmed. This is a serious escalation of the U.S.-Iran conflict we flagged last issue, and it makes an Iranian cyberattack somewhat more likely as a matter of motive. But motive is not evidence — nothing this week points to an actual Iranian cyberattack against U.S. infrastructure, so we are not raising our threat rating on that specific question yet.

Section II

Key Judgments

KJ-1
Russian government hackers will keep breaking into routers and network equipment that still have factory-default settings, and Texas organizations with older equipment or informal IT management carry the same risk demonstrated this week. HIGH CONFIDENCE
Source basis: CISA/NSA/FBI/DC3 joint advisory AA26-194A, 13 July 2026, co-signed by 19 agencies across 13 countries; same-day CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog addition. Technical detail: unauthenticated SNMPv1/v2 default community-string abuse against public-facing router management interfaces, followed by TFTP-based configuration exfiltration — no CVE or malware required. Primary uncertainty: no confirmed Texas-named victim identified in open reporting this week; Texas-specific exposure is an analytic extrapolation from sector targeting, not a confirmed intrusion.
Decision Implication: This week, get a list of every router and network device your company owns that can be reached from the internet. Confirm someone has permission to shut one off immediately if it’s found compromised, even if it’s in daily use.
KJ-2
The weak point isn’t routers alone — it’s any piece of equipment that sits on the edge of the network and connects to the internet, including the systems employees use for remote access. A second, unrelated attacker proved this the same week by breaking into different equipment the same way. HIGH CONFIDENCE
Source basis: SonicWall PSIRT advisory SNWLID-2026-0008, 14 July 2026, covering CVE-2026-15409 (unauthenticated SSRF, CVSS 10.0) and CVE-2026-15410 (post-authentication code injection); CISA KEV catalog addition, 14 July 2026, under BOD 26-04. Primary uncertainty: no attribution to a specific threat actor or group has been published for this exploitation; treat as criminal or unknown-actor activity, distinct from the Russian government attribution in KJ-1.
Decision Implication: Extend this week’s equipment inventory beyond routers to include any remote-access or VPN equipment. If your company uses SonicWall SMA1000 devices, update or disconnect them now — don’t wait for the next maintenance window.
KJ-3
Having a security-contact email posted on a website is not the same as having a working process. Organizations that haven’t actually tested how an outside report reaches a real decision-maker are at risk of the same failure that just happened to the federal government itself. HIGH CONFIDENCE
Source basis: CISA/NSA/JPCERT/NCSC-NL/NCSC-UK joint guidance on coordinated vulnerability disclosure programs, 15 July 2026; CISA’s own disclosure of its GovCloud-key incident, reported 9 July 2026. Primary uncertainty: this is a directly observed governance pattern at CISA itself, not an inference about adversary behavior; whether the pattern is widespread among Texas critical infrastructure operators remains an assessment pending client verification.
Decision Implication: This week, confirm your organization has a security-contact address, and actually send it a test message to see how long it takes a real person to respond. If nobody answers within a day or two, that’s the gap CISA just demonstrated.
KJ-4
Carried forward from ATB-2026-17/18: Iran likely still wants to retaliate against U.S. infrastructure with a cyberattack, and this week’s combat deaths make that motive stronger — but there is still no evidence an actual cyberattack has happened. MODERATE CONFIDENCE, UNCHANGED
Source basis: CENTCOM statements reported by CNN, NPR, Axios, Stars and Stripes, and Al Jazeera, 17–19 July 2026 (multi-source wire reporting, high reliability on the kinetic fact). Primary uncertainty: no CISA/FBI/NSA advisory or named-victim disclosure has corroborated Iranian cyber intensification — the specific evidence needed to raise this assessment remains outstanding. This is the fourth consecutive issue without that confirming evidence.
Decision Implication: No change to your security posture is required based on this week’s combat news alone. Keep your existing precautions in place around industrial systems and vendor connections — don’t relax them because the news feels quieter, and don’t tighten them further based on battlefield news that hasn’t produced any actual cyber evidence.
Section III

Geopolitical Driver

Two different countries are creating risk right now, but on very different levels of certainty, and it’s important not to blur them together. Russia’s router campaign is proven — confirmed by 19 government agencies with technical detail to back it up. The likely goal is quiet, long-term access they can use later, not an immediate attack. Iran is the opposite case: the real-world conflict is confirmed and getting worse, but no one has shown evidence of an actual Iranian cyberattack yet. Treating both threats the same way would be a mistake in either direction — underestimating what Russia has already proven it can do, or overreacting to an Iranian cyberattack that, so far, hasn’t happened.

Plain-language summary: Russia is quietly and proven to be getting into U.S. networks through unlocked doors. Iran is in an active shooting conflict with the U.S. and has a stronger motive than before to strike back with a cyberattack, but hasn’t done so yet, as far as anyone can confirm. Track them separately — don’t let the louder story (Iran) distract from the proven one (Russia).

Section IV

Why This Matters to Texas

The equipment named in this week’s warnings — routers, remote-access boxes, VPN equipment — sits underneath every sector Texas leadership tracks, but it’s rarely discussed at the board level because it’s treated as an IT detail rather than a business risk. This week says that framing is wrong: three separate incidents, three different attackers, one shared weak spot.

Cross-Sector Cascade Assessment

Energy
Power / Vendor Connections
What changed: The power sector is named directly in this week’s Russian router warning. Why it matters locally: A compromised router or remote-access box can knock out the connections vendors and technicians use to monitor and respond to outages — without ever touching the actual power equipment. Texas energy companies should treat “who owns our network equipment list” as a board question this week, not an IT ticket. Cascade risk: A power disruption ripples into hospitals, banks, and shipping within hours.
Financial
Branch Networks / Vendor Risk
What changed: Banking is named directly in the Russian router warning; the same week, federal charges confirmed banks were among the victims of the ransomware gangs tied to the indicted hosting operation. Why it matters locally: This is a double exposure — a foreign government and criminal ransomware gangs are both exploiting the same kind of weak spot. Cascade risk: Leadership should pre-approve a plan to quickly disconnect a compromised branch or vendor connection without losing the records needed for a later investigation.
Healthcare / Defense Contractors / AI
Continuity / Suppliers
Healthcare: Named in the Russian router warning and among this week’s federal indictment victims. Hospitals often rely on outside IT vendors and can’t easily tolerate downtime, which makes this exposure worse. Defense contractors: Also named directly. Smaller Texas-based suppliers with lean security teams are the likely weak link in the defense supply chain — a leadership and staffing gap fixable this week with a simple equipment count, not an expensive new purchase. Cascade risk: A hospital outage creates immediate patient-safety risk; a defense-supplier outage creates contract and national-security risk.
Section V

Indicators & Warnings — What We’re Watching, Next 1 to 4 Weeks

PIR 2 / IND 1 Actual proof of an Iranian cyberattack — not just motive ↑ Rising
  • We’re watching for a federal government warning, or a company publicly confirming it was hit, that specifically names Iran as the attacker.
  • That’s the specific evidence that would move our Iran assessment (KJ-4) from a “probably wants to” to a “confirmed doing it.”
  • Tied to: PIR 2, cross-sector risk.
PIR 1 / IND 2 A Texas company or agency named as a victim of either this week’s router campaign or the SonicWall attack ↑ Rising
  • We’re watching for any breach notification or advisory that names a specific Texas organization.
  • That would turn this week’s general warning (KJ-1, KJ-2) into a confirmed, local problem.
  • Tied to: PIR 1, targeting of Texas organizations specifically.
PIR 4 / IND 3 Whether the ransomware gangs find a new landlord → Sustained
  • We’re watching to see whether the ransomware gangs affected by this week’s federal charges simply move to new hosting providers.
  • Would tell us whether the charges actually disrupted them, or were just an inconvenience.
  • Tied to: PIR 4, criminal infrastructure resilience.
PIR 6 / IND 4 Whether another organization repeats CISA’s mistake → Sustained
  • We’re watching for another case where a security researcher’s warning gets ignored or mishandled at a company or agency.
  • Would tell us whether this week’s failure was a one-time slip at CISA, or a widespread problem.
  • Tied to: PIR 6, leadership-relevant governance warning.
PIR 3 / IND 5 Whether the Iran conflict spreads to places tied to Texas business ↑ Rising
  • We’re watching for strikes on Middle East infrastructure connected to Texas energy exports or defense contractors — a desalination plant in Kuwait has already been hit twice this week.
  • This would raise the urgency of the Iran story, though not by itself change our cyberattack confidence level in KJ-4.
  • Tied to: PIR 3 and PIR 7, escalation and conflict-driven cyber risk.
Section VI

Governance Implication Block

Decision at risk
Whether your organization can name, in writing, one person who owns the list of internet-connected network equipment, and one person who owns handling an outside security report. Both gaps caused every incident described in this issue — including the federal government’s own.
Owner
Chief Information Security Officer, or whoever runs IT infrastructure, with the board’s risk committee kept in the loop given how many sectors this week’s warnings named.
Consequence of delay
An unlocked digital door stays open at the exact moment a second country’s motive to retaliate is getting stronger — and there’s no clear way for an outside researcher or partner to warn you about a problem before it becomes public.
Action this week
Count every router, firewall, and remote-access device connected to the internet, SonicWall SMA1000 devices included. Confirm who can disconnect one immediately. Test your security-contact process — don’t just publish it.
Record to preserve
A dated, named record of who reviewed this week’s warnings and what they decided about each piece of equipment found exposed. Proof that your security-contact process was actually tested, not just posted online.
From Warning to Decision

Would your leadership team act in time?

Reading the warning is one thing. Making the decision with incomplete information and the clock running is another.

Section VII

Actions This Week

Ask: Can we name, right now, who owns our network-equipment list and who owns handling an outside security report?

Approve: A same-week count of every router, firewall, and remote-access device connected to the internet, with a decision written down for each one found exposed.

Document: A dated, named record of this week’s review, and proof that your security-contact process was actually tested.

Rehearse: Not needed this cycle — this is a “get organized” fix, not a drill.

Section VIII

Prior Judgment Tracker

Prior judgment
Last issue (ATB-2026-18), we said Iran’s cyber-retaliation risk was “probably wants to but hasn’t yet,” and named “further U.S.-Iran fighting” as the specific event that would push us to treat this as an active crisis for Gulf-connected Texas industries.
Current status
That event happened. The U.S. military confirmed three American combat deaths in Jordan and Iraq this week, with a fourth pending confirmation. The fighting itself is confirmed and serious. But the specific thing we said would raise our cyberattack confidence — actual evidence of an Iranian cyberattack — still hasn’t shown up. We’re holding the line on that distinction this week.
What changed
The bigger story this week wasn’t Iran. It was three separate, unrelated incidents — the Russian router campaign, the SonicWall attack, and the federal government’s own security-reporting failure — all pointing to the same root problem: basic equipment and process management.
Confidence movement
Three new high-confidence findings this issue, all about the equipment and process problem (KJ-1, KJ-2, KJ-3). The Iran cyberattack assessment (KJ-4) stays exactly where it was — we’re not letting dramatic battlefield news push up a cyber-risk number without actual cyber evidence.
Next indicator
A government warning or a confirmed victim naming Iran specifically is still what would change our Iran assessment. A Texas organization named as a victim of this week’s router or remote-access attacks would turn a general warning into a local, confirmed problem.

// Torch Fusion Cycle — ATB-2026-19

WHAT: The week of 12–18 July 2026 came down to one theme: unlocked doors, everywhere. Russia broke into routers with default passwords. A separate, unrelated attacker broke into remote-access equipment through a known flaw. Federal prosecutors charged the hosting operation behind four major ransomware gangs. And the federal government admitted its own security-reporting process failed a researcher for over a week — right before publishing advice on how to avoid exactly that. Separately, the U.S. and Iran had their first confirmed combat deaths of the renewed conflict. WHO: Russian government hackers ran the proven, confirmed campaign. A separate, unidentified attacker exploited the remote-access flaw. A Russian hosting operation and its ransomware clients ran the criminal thread. Iran is the country behind the military conflict, with no confirmed cyber piece yet. WHY: All three cyber stories trace back to the same root cause: equipment and processes that nobody is actively managing, at organizations of every size, including the federal government itself. The Iran story matters because it strengthens, without yet proving, a threat we’ve now been watching for four straight issues without new evidence. WHAT NEXT: Leadership should treat this week as the nudge to assign real owners — for equipment and for handling security reports — rather than waiting for a Texas company to show up in the headlines first. Warnings that arrive too late are not warnings. They are after-action reports.
